lead: A load that arrives in a very short time stresses a part far more than the same load applied slowly. A weight dropped on a collar stretches the rod much further than the same weight hung gently, because at the lowest point the weight has stopped and the rod has taken up the whole loss of potential energy, W(h + δ), as strain energy. The impact factor compares the dynamic stress with the static one. Crane hooks, lift cages, hammers, railway buffers and machine mounts are designed with it. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic; most treat it as an application of strain energy.
prereq: You need: axial extension δ = PL/(AE) and beam deflection (see Direct, bending and torsional stresses, and Static, dynamic and impact loads), and the chapter on theories of failure for comparing the result with a strength.

blocks.text: Take a vertical rod of length L, area A and Young's modulus E, so its stiffness is k = AE/L. A weight W hung slowly gives the static extension δ<sub>st</sub> = W/k = WL/(AE) and the static stress σ<sub>st</sub> = W/A. Units: W in N, L and δ in mm, A in mm², E in N/mm² (MPa).

Applied suddenly (released from touching the collar, with no drop), the weight does work Wδ while the rod stores only ½kδ², so δ = 2δ<sub>st</sub> and σ = 2σ<sub>st</sub>. The rod overshoots to twice the static stretch and then oscillates.
Dropped through a height h, the weight does work W(h + δ) by the time it stops. Equating this to ½kδ² gives a quadratic in δ whose positive root is:

The bracket is the impact factor. At h = 0 it is 2, the sudden load. When h is much larger than δ<sub>st</sub> it is close to √(2h/δ<sub>st</sub>), so a stiff part (small δ<sub>st</sub>) feels a large factor.

The formula assumes the rod stays elastic, the rod's own mass is neglected, the stress is uniform along the rod at every instant (no stress waves), the weight stays in contact and no energy is lost as heat or sound. Leaving out the rod's mass errs slightly on the safe side when the weight is much heavier than the rod; for very fast impacts on long bars, stress waves make the real peak higher than the formula gives.

The strain energy stored in the rod at stress σ is U = σ²AL/(2E). The modulus of resilience is the energy per unit volume up to yield, u<sub>r</sub> = S<sub>yt</sub>²/(2E); the modulus of toughness is the energy per unit volume up to fracture, the whole area under the stress–strain curve. A part that must absorb shock should have a large stressed volume and a low working stress, which is why bolts for shock loads are turned down to the root diameter of the thread along their shank.

Shock loading means any load applied in a very short time, once or many times: a hammer blow, a cam follower hitting its cam, a lorry crossing a joint. Design multiplies the static load by an impact or service factor and then checks strength and, if the shocks repeat, fatigue. A spring or rubber pad adds deflection for the same force, so δ<sub>st</sub> grows and the impact factor falls; the second worked example shows how much.

examples.question: A 500 N weight falls 50 mm onto a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel rod 20 mm in diameter and 1 m long. E = 200 GPa. Find the static extension, the impact factor, the maximum extension and the maximum stress.
steps: σ = Eδ/L = 200 000 × 0.900/1000 = 180.0 MPa, against a static stress of 500/314.16 = 1.59 MPa.
examples.answer: δ = 0.90 mm and σ = 180 MPa, 113 times the static stress. A steel with S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa stays elastic, but only just with a factor of 1.4.

examples.question: To protect the rod of the first example, a helical spring of stiffness 2000 N/mm is fitted on the collar, so the weight now lands on the spring. Find the new maximum stress in the rod.
steps: Spring and rod act in series: 1/k<sub>eq</sub> = 1/62 832 + 1/2000, so k<sub>eq</sub> = 1938.3 N/mm.
The spring shortens by 10 357/2000 = 5.18 mm and the rod stretches by 10 357/62 832 = 0.165 mm.
examples.answer: The rod stress falls from 180 MPa to about 33 MPa: the soft spring takes the energy over a 5.2 mm stroke instead of 0.9 mm.

traps: Taking the impact factor as 1 for a suddenly applied load. It is 2.
Writing the work as Wh only. The weight keeps falling while the rod stretches, so the work is W(h + δ).
Mixing units in 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>: h in metres and δ<sub>st</sub> in millimetres throws the root off by a factor of about 30.
Thinking a stronger, stiffer rod always helps. A smaller δ<sub>st</sub> raises the impact factor; extra flexibility often helps more than extra strength.

quiz.q: Define the impact factor and give its value for a suddenly applied load.
quiz.a: The ratio of the maximum dynamic stress (or extension) to the static value under the same load; it is 2 for a sudden load.

quiz.q: Why does a suddenly applied load give twice the static extension?
quiz.a: The full load W does work Wδ as the rod stretches, but the rod stores only ½kδ². Equating them gives δ = 2W/k = 2δ<sub>st</sub>.

quiz.q: A rod of area 200 mm² carries a 1 kN load applied suddenly. Find the maximum stress.
Why does a rubber pad reduce the impact stress in a rod?
quiz.a: It adds deflection for the same force, so δ<sub>st</sub> rises and h/δ<sub>st</sub> falls. The impact factor 1 + √(1 + 2h/δ<sub>st</sub>) falls with it.

quiz.q: Define modulus of resilience and modulus of toughness.
quiz.a: Resilience: strain energy per unit volume up to yield, S<sub>yt</sub>²/(2E). Toughness: energy per unit volume up to fracture, the area under the stress–strain curve.

quiz.q: Find the modulus of resilience of a steel with S<sub>yt</sub> = 250 MPa and E = 200 GPa.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical impact design uses transient finite element analysis with strain-rate-dependent material data, and drop tests on the real product. Shock mounts are chosen by energy absorbed per unit volume and by heat build-up under repeated shocks. Search for 'drop test', 'shock isolator' and 'strain-rate sensitivity'.
